newsitem.title: EAST TIMOR: E.Timor statue ceremony passes off peacefully.
newsitem.headline: E.Timor statue ceremony passes off peacefully.

text.p: Nobel laureate Bishop Carlos Belo blessed a giant statue of Jesus Christ in the troubled territory of East Timor on Sunday in a ceremony which passed off without feared political protests.

Residents had said restive youths in the former Portuguese colony might protest against Indonesia's 1975 annexation of the territory but more than 15,000 people at the ceremony watched in near-silence, occasionally bursting into applause.
The only unusual event was a fire on an adjacent hill as the ceremony ended, apparently ignited by a cigarette butt thrown onto the dry grass. Despite the blaze the crowd remained quiet.

The only policemen seen were a handful who accompanied Belo to the bottom of the headland some seven km (3 miles) from the East Timor capital Dili, on top of which the 27-metre (90-foot) bronze statue is located.

The bishop, dressed in a white cassock, climbed up steps cut into the hill to the base of the statue along with other priests and local officials and the regional military commander. There he said a short prayer and blessed the statue with holy water and incense, his robe waving in the wind.
In a sermon later, he said: "This location, starting from this moment on, will become a sacred place for the people of East Timor to come and pray and meditate.
"I hope this symbol of the statue of Christ the King will become a symbol for lovers of truth, justice and peace," he said in the Indonesian language.
Mainly Moslem Indonesia invaded predominantly Roman Catholic East Timor in 1975 and annexed it the following year in a move never recognised by the United Nations.
Sporadic resistance to Jakarta's rule still erupts in the territory and some 200 guerillas are said to be still holed up in the dry, rugged hills in the interior.
Indonesia maintains a disproportionate military presence in East Timor compared to its neighbouring provinces, saying that the troops are needed to help development of the territory.
The troubles in East Timor have grabbed world attention since Belo and self-exiled resistance leader Jose Ramos-Horta were jointly awarded the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize last month.

Belo, perhaps the most-respected person in the territory, has strived to walk a tightrope between his disgruntled flock and Indonesian authorities. He had previously indicated that he wanted no political protests during Sunday's ceremony.

The statue, the largest of Christ outside Rio de Janeiro in Brazil, has angered the East Timorese. It was built by the Jakarta government and paid for by the national flag carrier Garuda Indonesia and is seen as a symbol of Indonesia's rule.
Many residents say it was conceived as a tourist attraction rather than a religious monument.
